25 years since Tiananmen Square massacre, China not ready to confront its past

Lindy Kerin reported this story on Wednesday, June 4, 2014 12:46:00

← Full The World Today episode — Wednesday, 4 June 2014

Listen to The World Today

Audio of this The World Today story, as originally broadcast.

ELEANOR HALL: Twenty-five years ago today, China's government ordered the army to open fire on unarmed student protesters in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

There has never been an official account of how many people were slaughtered but some dissidents estimate that 3,000 people were killed by their own government that day.

Ever since the government has banned any mention of the protest in an attempt to erase it from the country's collective memory.

As Lindy Kerin reports.

LINDY KERIN: In 1989 after more than six weeks of pro-democracy demonstrations, the Chinese government ordered the army to move.

Thousands of troops accompanied by tanks and army trucks flooded Tiananmen Square. They shot and crushed anyone who got in the way.

This is how the ABC's Peter Cave reported what happened.

(Sound of gunfire)

PETER CAVE (archival): A long column of reinforcement troops are moving into the square now. People are throwing things at them and as you can hear, they are returning the thrown insults and bottles and stones with gunfire.

(Sound of gunfire)

LINDY KERIN: Today the events are still vivid for the veteran journalist.

PETER CAVE: I remember being asleep in my hotel room and about 10 o'clock at night and I heard some sort of commotion going on outside the window and I pulled the curtain back and I looking out of the window and there was an APC (armoured personnel carrier) showering sparks as it went across the barricade squashing the young students who'd been out there for weeks manning the barricades, squashing their bikes and I knew it was on. I knew this was it.

LINDY KERIN: The Tiananmen Square massacre is still etched in the minds of many around the world but the Chinese government has attempted to erase it from the memories of its people.

There will be no official commemorations there today.

Instead security has been stepped up. Amnesty International says at least 66 people have been detained in connection to the anniversary, including Chinese Australian artist Guo Jian.

Meanwhile, a group of French journalists has been detained and interrogated for six hours. Their alleged crime: being on the streets interviewing people about the events of 25 years ago.

The foreign affairs spokesman Hong Lei issued this warning to foreign reporters.

HONG LEI (translated): Regarding foreign journalists, we have presented our position many times. The Chinese side is willing to support the legal reporting conducted by foreign journalists in China. We also request that foreign journalists follow Chinese laws.

LINDY KERIN: China watcher Dr Pradeep Taneja is from the University of Melbourne's School of Political Sciences. He says while the economic situation in China has changed significantly, many things haven't.

PRADEEP TANEJA: Life is certainly is much better in terms of living standards and in economic terms, but in terms of political freedom, yes they're able to read about, you know, various ideas and theories in social sciences or talk about various things, except, as I said, there are certain taboo subjects and Tiananmen Square is one of those incidents that people don't read about.

For example, outside China, people have seen pictures of the tank man, you know, from the day after the Tiananmen Square massacre, but within China, people don't know that image exists, or what that actually means. There have been experiments where foreign journalists or academics have shown that picture to Chinese university students and they have no idea what this picture is about.

LINDY KERIN: Do you think there will ever be a time when the country does want to confront its past?

PRADEEP TANEJA: I'm sure there will come a time when the Chinese people will have to face up to this, the incident of 1989 but this is not the time. I mean for the Chinese Communist Party this is a very sensitive issue.

This is a blot on their record. I mean they have certainly delivered, you know, improvements in living standards for the Chinese people, quite considerable improvement, but when it comes to this particular event, I think sooner or later the Chinese people will have to face up to it.

LINDY KERIN: Chai Ling was one of the leaders of the protests back in 1989. She now lives in Boston in the United States.

She's told the BBC she was caught completely by surprise when the tanks rolled in.

CHAI LING: I think what shocked Chinese people, shocked the world. What kind of government, what kind of army would open fire at armless, peaceful student and citizens? To use tank strips to run them over.

LINDY KERIN: Chai Ling was put on the country's most wanted list and lived in hiding for almost a year.

She says there's still a reluctance to confront what happened in China but she says eventually that will change.

CHAI LING: Do I have hope and faith for this new generation student who has grown up in materialism? I do. I believe that when the time is right, these kids are going to want to find what's the truth.

ELEANOR HALL: That's Tiananmen Square protestor, Chai Ling ending Lindy Kerin's report.
